newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ANALYSTS' COMMENTS ON KLM H1 PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS' COMMENTS ON KLM H1 PROFITS.

text.p: KLM Royal Dutch Airlines on Tuesday reported a drop in operating profits for the first half of its 1996/97 financial year to 262 million guilders from 497.
The following are analysts' comments:
Thibaud de Guerre, analyst at ING Barings Research -

"The bottom line was slightly above my expactations but the results are not of a very good quality. Half the net comes from its stake in Northwest Airlines, this shows the core activities of KLM are not producing a profit any more.
The restructuring programme is badly needed to compensate tariff pressure from market liberalisation in Europe."
One London-based analyst who asked not to be named:

"It's rather disappointing. The profit was largely in line with our expectations, but the operating performance has gone badly wrong. They're putting in cost-cutting, but they've lost the edge. How will they catch up with BA and Lufthansa. They're about six months behind."
Frits de Vries, analyst at brokers Gilissen -

"I'm a bit disappointed but then our expectations were already low. The big worry is the rise in costs other than fuel in the second quarter -- that was unexpected. I have my doubts the company will be able to realise the cost savings it has set. Around 500 million guilders is possible but 1.5 billion guilders is going to be very difficult.
Bangert & Pontier analyst Paul Schram said he was likely to trim his estimates for KLM, but not before a planned conference call later today.
He noticed an unexpected rise in "other" operational costs, operational lease costs, landing costs, and sub-contractor costs, which, he said, totalled some 100 million guilders.
"I'd expected wage and fuel costs to rise, but this came as a bad surprise to me."
Schram said strong measures were necessary to bring down the break-even load factor.

Plans to save 1.5 billion guilders over three years via the Focus 2000 restructuring were, Schram said, a positive step and lent support to KLM shares, but he was uncertain where KLM would get the savings from.
"The load factor can be brought up a little, especially in cargo, but the main savings must come from cost-cutting.
"I expect the ratio of staff relative to cabin personnel will be reduced".
Juergen Pieper, transport analyst at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt -

"My reaction is that the numbers are more or less as expected. There are two things to say on the positive side. Firstly, it's not a catastrophe. Secondly, their load factors have been increasing for three months now.

But compare with other major airlines, notably BA and Lufthansa, and KLM is clearly doing worse. Its net profit has gained year-on-year, but it is down on EBIT (earnings before interest and tax). The high fuel costs may explain the weaker quarter, but the others are doing a better job.

They still have a major problem of controlling costs, especially on the personnel side. I'm waiting for an improvement. The short-term evaluation is quite low and, in the long term, we remain cautious.
We would need to see a serious restructuring or a strengthening with other airlines. KLM was the first to join with a U.S. airline, but they are now behind."
Charles Estourgie, analyst at Kempen & Co -

"The only way to achieve big cost savings will be to work on a larger scale, especially in the commodity business. KLM only has an (overall) market share of 6.5 percent in Europe and said earlier it wanted to reach a 10 percent coverage in Europe. Since the company announced today it would halt expansion of its European fleet, the only solution will be to find a partner. I would not be surprised if there was news on this quite soon."
--Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
